summary.heading: Charge, current and potential difference
summary.html:
• Charge is quantised (whole numbers of $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ C) and conserved. Like charges repel, unlike attract.
  • Conductors have many mobile charge carriers (free electrons in metals, ions in solutions); insulators have almost none; semiconductors have few, and more with heat or light.
$$I = \frac{\Delta q}{\Delta t} \qquad V = \frac{W}{q}$$
  • Direct current: a flow of charge carriers in one direction. $1\ \text{A} = 1\ \text{C s}^{-1}$. Conventional current goes from + to −; electrons in a metal drift the other way, slowly (typically under a mm per second), but all start moving at once.
  • P.d.: work done per unit charge moving positive charge between two points. $1\ \text{V} = 1\ \text{J C}^{-1}$. Always between two points, never "through".
  • Circuit symbols are in the data booklet. Ammeter in series (ideal: zero resistance); voltmeter in parallel (ideal: infinite resistance). Meters are ideal unless stated; a non-ideal meter has a given, constant resistance.

summary.heading: Resistance, resistivity and Ohm's law
summary.html:
$$R = \frac{V}{I} \qquad \rho = \frac{RA}{L}$$
  • Origin of resistance: drifting electrons collide with vibrating lattice ions and give them kinetic energy, so the metal heats up (the heating effect). Hotter metal: more vibration, more collisions, more resistance.
  • Resistivity $\rho$ (Ω m) depends only on the material (and temperature). Longer wire, more $R$; thicker wire, less.
  • Ohm's law: $I \propto V$ for a conductor at constant temperature (and other conditions). Such a component is ohmic; a metal at constant temperature is ohmic.
  • $R = \dfrac{V}{I}$ defines resistance for any component; Ohm's law adds that $R$ stays constant.
  • Filament lamp (non-ohmic): more current, hotter filament, larger $R$, so the I–V graph curves over (same shape reversed). Find $R$ from $\dfrac{V}{I}$ at a point, not from the gradient.

summary.heading: Electrical power
summary.html:
$$P = IV = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R}$$
  • Choose the form with the quantities you know. In a resistor all the power is dissipated as thermal energy.

summary.heading: Series and parallel circuits
summary.html:
SeriesParallel
current$I = I_1 = I_2$$I = I_1 + I_2$
p.d.$V = V_1 + V_2$$V = V_1 = V_2$
resistance$R_s = R_1 + R_2$$\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2}$
  • From conservation of charge (current into a junction = current out) and conservation of energy (round a loop, p.d.s add up to the emf).
  • Adding a resistor in series increases the total; in parallel it decreases it. $R_p$ is smaller than the smallest branch; two equal resistors in parallel give half of one.

summary.heading: Variable resistors and potential dividers
summary.html:
• The guide limits variable resistors to three. Thermistor (NTC, semiconductor): hotter, lower resistance. LDR (semiconductor): brighter light, lower resistance. Potentiometer: a sliding contact gives any fraction of the p.d.
$$V_{\text{out}} = V_{\text{in}} \times \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$$
  • Two resistors in series share the supply p.d. in proportion to their resistances ($V \propto R$, same current). Not in the data booklet: be ready to derive it. With a thermistor or LDR as one resistor, it makes a sensor circuit.

summary.heading: Cells, emf and internal resistance
summary.html:
• The emf $\varepsilon$ is the work done per unit charge by a source in moving charge round the complete circuit: energy converted into electrical energy per coulomb (in volts; not a force). P.d. is electrical energy converted into other forms in a component.
  • Chemical cells: reactions between two electrodes and an electrolyte. Primary cells are used once; secondary cells are rechargeable (current pushed backwards reverses the reactions). A battery is cells in series: emfs add.
$$\varepsilon = I(R + r)$$
  • Terminal p.d. $V = IR = \varepsilon - Ir$ ($Ir$ is the "lost volts", which warms the cell). With no current, $V = \varepsilon$.
  • Measuring $\varepsilon$ and $r$: vary $R$, record $I$ and $V$, plot $V$ against $I$: a straight line, $V = -rI + \varepsilon$, with gradient $-r$ and $y$-intercept $\varepsilon$.

summary.heading: Solar cells and comparing sources
summary.html:
• Solar (photovoltaic) cell: layers of semiconductor (usually treated silicon); absorbed photons free electrons that are driven round the circuit. Output depends on light intensity (weather, time of day, season, angle); nothing at night. Panels convert about 20% of the incident light.
  • Primary cells: portable, cheap, steady p.d.; little energy stored, not rechargeable, harmful waste.
  • Secondary cells: portable, reusable, store renewable energy; costly, slow to charge, lose capacity, mining costs (lithium, cobalt).
  • Solar cells: renewable, no emissions or fuel while running, low maintenance, good in remote places; intermittent, large area, energy and materials to make.
  • Mains: large, continuous, cheap per kWh; not portable, often from fossil fuels (enhanced greenhouse effect, B.2).

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• Saying current is "used up". Current is the same either side of a series component; energy is transferred.
  • Meters in the wrong place (ammeters in series, voltmeters in parallel).
  • Forgetting to invert $\frac{1}{R_p}$.
  • Using the diameter in $A = \pi r^2$, or not converting mm to m.
  • Taking resistance from the gradient of a curved I–V graph.
  • Calling $V = IR$ Ohm's law.
  • Confusing emf with terminal p.d. (equal only when $I = 0$).
  • Getting thermistors and LDRs backwards.
  • Mixing up conventional current and electron flow.

Models: The "electrons bumping into ions" picture explains why resistance rises with temperature. What does it fail to explain (for example, why a thermistor does the opposite)?
Compare thermal and electrical conduction in metals. What does the shared free-electron model predict about materials that are good at one but not the other?
Conventions: Franklin's choice of which charge to call positive was a 50–50 guess that turned out the "wrong" way for metals. Should physics switch to electron flow now? List what it would cost.
Find other conventions in physics (sign conventions in B.4, positive direction in A.1). What makes a good convention?
Measurement and patterns: Ohm's 1827 results were at first received coolly in Germany, where critics distrusted his mathematical approach. What would students need to see before believing a new law from one person's data?
Ask students to sketch the I–V graph they would expect for a lamp before measuring. How does a pattern become a law?
Global impact: Cheaper batteries and solar panels are changing energy use worldwide. Who benefits first, and who pays the environmental costs of mining?
Can a physics improvement (for example, more efficient solar cells) on its own solve an environmental problem?

oracy.html:
Talk tokens (fours, 10 minutes): each student spends a token to add each step of the explanation; nobody speaks again until everyone has spent one. Claim: "With two different lamps in series with a cell, the lamp nearer the positive terminal is brighter, because current is used up on the way round."

  • The next step is …
  • That fits with …, because …
  • I'd change one word: …

Listen for: charge is conserved, so the current is the same everywhere in series; energy is transferred, not current, and swapping the lamps changes nothing.

Does it matter that conventional current: If two descriptions (conventional current and electron flow) always give the same predictions, is one of them more true?
Where else does knowledge rest on an agreed convention (a map's north at the top, the order of a calendar)?
Can we know what we can't observe?: List the meter readings and experiments that lead us to believe in drifting electrons. At which step does observation become inference?
Does it change students' confidence to learn that a typical drift speed is under a millimetre per second?
When is a \"law\" not a law?: Ohm's law describes some materials only. Compare it with conservation of charge, which has no known exceptions. Should they share the word "law"?
Who decides what gets called a law, a principle or a rule in science?
Who decides which energy source is best?: Give groups one energy source each to defend. Which of their arguments could be settled by measurement, and which could not?
Should the cheapest source win if its costs fall on other countries or future generations?
